You are the controller for CIVIC (this repo). The owner wants CIVIC rebuilt on the same foundations and lessons as their other project, Orca (/Users/taymoor/Projects/orca), and two new features built. Read CIVIC's AGENTS.md, docs/product-spec.md, docs/roadmap.md, docs/decisions/, and docs/self-dogfood.md (your base branch `docs/source-to-element` adds a section "Still to build: source-to-element and backend coverage" — read it first). Run `entire brain brief` per AGENTS/agent guide if present.

## Owner direction (15 Nov 2026)
1. CIVIC should be an **Effect.ts (v4) + XState (v6) + Electron** project, like Orca.
2. CIVIC should **be an MCP server itself**, with **agent/harness integrations** (it already has an MCP server and a Claude Code/Codex plugin under integrations/ — build on them). Keep decision 0006: CIVIC makes no model calls and launches no agents; integrations mean plugins/skills/MCP that harnesses use, not CIVIC driving agents.
3. Build the two features in docs/self-dogfood.md: **source-to-element** (select element → source file/line, and file/diff → elements; carried on comments and work requests; try on CIVIC's own UI first) and **backend coverage** (routes/handlers/RPCs each journey exercises, and which none reach; derived from recorded runs + graph, never hand lists). CIVIC already reviews itself as the "Isolated CIVIC" workspace via `civic preview`; making CIVIC a project in its own picker is now needed. Reference only (not a dependency): Gui, https://usegui.com (Apache 2.0) for element→source mapping.
4. **Clean up the codebase** using Orca's lessons (below).

## Order
First deliver a written plan (docs/plans/…): audit of CIVIC's current architecture vs the target (Effect services/layers, XState machines for lifecycles like preview/review/request, Electron shell, MCP surface, integrations), what to keep, the migration in small landable slices with tests, and where the two features land in that order. Prefer doing the features on the new foundations rather than building them twice. Then execute slice by slice. Decide within this direction yourself; only real owner calls (spend, sign-in, security, product direction changes) go to the owner. Report in plain everyday words.

## Lessons from Orca to apply (read the referenced Orca files; Orca is read-only for you)
- **Effect + XState pattern:** Orca's durable XState kernel `apps/server/src/core/machine/kernel.ts` (+ kernel.test.ts) and landing machine `apps/server/src/core/landing/machine.ts` (+ machine.test.ts); architecture plan `git -C /Users/taymoor/Projects/orca show w/xstate-plan:docs/plans/2026-11-15-xstate-engine.md` (incl. @xstate/effect persistence and timers addendum). XState v6 alpha graph tests require every event to be covered. Effect audits: `git -C /Users/taymoor/Projects/orca show w/code-audit:docs/research/2026-11-15-effect-usage-audit.md` and `…-codebase-quality-audit.md`, `…-react-effects-audit.md`.
- **Corrections become checks** (Lauren Tan's talk): turn every recurring review correction into a lint rule/test/gate with a committed baseline that may only shrink — no `useEffect`, no raw `setTimeout`/`setInterval` (Effect Schedule/Clock), no `vi.mock`, architecture/layering rules across all src, short "why"-only comments, Effect language service diagnostics. No hardcoded lists of files/scripts/tools — derive them.
- **Tests are e2e and unmocked** (Playwright / real processes / temp data); misbehaving-agent style tests before any real-agent run.
- **Vite+ all the way:** `vp lint` (oxlint), `vp fmt` (oxfmt), `vp test`, `vp run` tasks + cache, `vp staged` + `vp hooks` (pre-commit lint check-only; commit-msg requires conventional types `fix:`/`feat:`/`refactor:`/…). See Orca's `scripts/commit-type.ts`, `.vite-hooks/` (chains each clone's own .git/hooks so Entire keeps working) once landed on Orca main. Deps: `pnpx taze major -r -l`, caret ranges, `pnpm audit`, installs only in worktrees.
- **Sign off and land small:** every change passes its own checks + full suites before landing; land each verified slice immediately; never batch unrelated work. Orca uses `scripts/signoff.ts` (sign off the exact commit, domain map, reuse) — CIVIC has `bin/signoff`; strengthen it rather than invent.
- **Resource frugality:** idle near-zero CPU; bounded caches/stores with cleanup; hunt leaks (the live CIVIC store `.civic-canvas/projects` holds 79 stale `orca-worktree-*` entries — fix the source of that growth; do not delete owner data without approval).
- **Owner-facing text:** everyday words, no IDs/paths/internals except behind "Details".
- **Harness integrations:** support the providers T3 Code supports plus any ACP agent; no hardcoded per-harness tool lists; verify by behaviour; lean on harness-native features.

## Working rules
- You are the controller: delegate independent implementation slices to Codex workers via T3 `delegate_task` (model gpt-6.1-sol, `isolation: "worktree"`), Opus architects/reviews. Pace usage over the week (don't drain weekly limits in 3 days); medium effort by default.
- Load gate before heavy runs: 1-min load < 6, one heavy test lane, ≤2 test workers. Orca's sign-offs share this machine — check `pgrep -f '[s]cripts/signoff\.ts( |$)'` and avoid running heavy suites at the same time.
- Safety: never change HOME; ephemeral ports only (never 3012, 3013, 4317, 5733, 4417, 5734, 10448, 10449); never touch the running 3012 instance or `.civic-canvas/` without owner approval; CIVIC's main checkout is the owner's live working copy — work in worktrees; never push or open PRs without the owner; signed commits only (1Password) — if signing fails, stop and say so; no secrets in logs.
- Keep working through the plan unattended (overnight too); end a turn only when everything remaining is genuinely blocked on the owner.

# Working on CIVIC

CIVIC is a deterministic product review and evidence system. Keep changes small,
maintainable, and grounded in the current checkout. Read the relevant package's
README and architecture decisions before changing its boundaries.

## Resource use is a product requirement

- Respect the user's time, CPU, RAM, disk, tokens, and subscriptions, both while
  developing CIVIC and while CIVIC runs on an end user's device.
- CIVIC makes no model calls. Agents and their subscriptions remain external
  ([decision 0006](docs/decisions/0006-deterministic-civic-for-agentic-teams.md)).
- Load projects and versions on demand. Search the running instance's loaded
  project; do not eagerly parse, build, or index every connected checkout.
- Bound concurrency and result sizes. Cancel abandoned requests, pause background
  polling/capture, and release browsers, workers, hosts, and subscriptions when
  their owners finish. Reuse expensive processes while work is queued; preserve
  per-preview storage and runtime isolation.
- Reuse valid captures and builds with explicit source/content, screen, viewport,
  and render-option identities. Bound cache retention and handle invalidation;
  never trade stale evidence for apparent speed.
- Loading states explain waiting; they do not establish a performance improvement.
  Measure the affected workload before claiming one. Include cold/warm behavior
  and cleanup when introducing expensive infrastructure or dependencies.
- Investigate narrowly and reuse results. Run focused checks first, then broaden
  only for changed risk or a required gate. Avoid duplicate builds, full captures,
  broad agent teams, and repeated unchanged polling.

## Ownership, isolation, and evidence

- Inspect the checkout, branch, diff, active runtime, and ownership before editing
  or restarting anything. Preserve unrelated changes and other agents' work.
- Connected app checkouts, dependencies, credentials, and production data are
  read-only unless the user explicitly authorizes changes to that source.
  Previews use CIVIC-owned snapshots, synthetic data, and disposable runtime state.
- Never silently install into, switch, reset, or clean an app's working tree.
  Failed or changing builds retain the previous usable preview and its evidence.
- Keep unsaved drafts, captures, comments, and recordings across navigation and
  resizing. Preserve existing confirmation guards for destructive replacement.
- Branch names and equal commit SHAs do not prove identical local contents.
  Bind evidence to recorded content and keep checkout selection explicit.
- Distinguish declared paths, static specimens, synthetic execution, replay,
  installed-app checks, and real-device/deployment acceptance. Report limits.
- Keep access keys and credentials out of logs, screenshots, exports, and commits.
  Preserve authentication, origin checks, loopback defaults, and Electron sandboxing.
- Keep connected-project adapters, designs, screenshots, and real-project validation
  reports in ignored local storage. Tracked examples and checks must be synthetic
  and must not require a named private project or a developer-specific checkout.
- Delete only verified, owned, regenerable artifacts within a checked boundary.
  Preserve source and evidence; respect deletion guards and external ownership.

## Shared implementation

| Area | Owner |
| --- | --- |
| Canvas, picker, screen review, search | `packages/canvas/` |
| Shared shadcn/Base UI controls, tokens, camera, review server | `packages/shell/` |
| Project connection, inventory, source/history discovery | `packages/vite-connector/` |
| Local app adapters, preview hosts, Electron lifecycle | `packages/local/` |
| Graph, import, review records, discovery | `graph/`, `importers/`, `review/`, `crawl/` |

- Fix shared behavior in its owner rather than duplicating project-specific or
  browser/Electron implementations. Keep app-specific behavior in adapters.
- Use shared shadcn/Base UI components and semantic tokens for shell UI. Preserve
  accessibility, focus, keyboard behavior, contrast, and narrow-window usability.
  Remove replaced legacy controls instead of retaining competing implementations.
- React Compiler belongs in CIVIC's Vite configuration, scoped to CIVIC's UI.
  Use memoization where it helps; avoid blanket wrappers and unstable Suspense
  promises. Preserve cancellation, error handling, and live frame identity.
- `packages/pnpm-workspace.yaml` and `packages/pnpm-lock.yaml` own the engine
  workspace. Use package scripts and declared versions; do not invent a root
  workspace or assume another app's dependency layout.

## Verification and delivery

- Start with the affected package's `check` and focused tests. For shell changes,
  verify the changed flow at desktop and narrow widths; verify Electron when its
  shared UI or lifecycle changes. Reuse existing acceptance scripts and fixtures.
- Every check runs under `bin/with-temp-root.mjs` (package `test` scripts and
  `bin/signoff` already do): its temp folder is removed afterwards, since one
  Electron profile is up to 110 MB. A new script that runs checks must go
  through it; `review/test/temp-root.test.ts` fails if one does not. Set
  `CIVIC_KEEP_TEMP=1` to keep a run's folder as evidence. Git inside it never
  signs, so checks do not ask the owner's signing key for fixture commits.
- Use temporary stores, profiles, ports, and synthetic data for acceptance.
  Do not disturb installed dogfood sessions or another owner's backend.
- When landing is authorized, sign off the exact committed candidate with
  `bin/signoff --no-post` from a clean checkout. That is a release gate, not a
  reason to rerun every suite during each edit. Do not stash someone else's work.
- Commit, merge, push, publish statuses, or dispatch GitHub CI only within the
  user's authorization. Preserve unrelated work when grouping commits.
- CIVIC merges its own branches: a CIVIC session makes a signed merge after
  `bin/signoff` on the result. A coordinator in another tool must not request
  integration into this repository (for example Orca's `orca_integrate`), and
  must leave `.civic/` and the owner's untracked root `package.json` alone.
- Report what changed, the checks actually run, and material remaining risks.
  Keep private validation evidence in ignored local storage; keep these instructions short.

See [README.md](README.md), [architecture decisions](docs/decisions), and the
[local runtime guide](packages/local/README.md) for details. Machine paths,
process IDs, ports, and historical signoffs are evidence, not current defaults.

# CIVIC reviewing CIVIC: the self-dogfood loop

Plan, 2026-10-23. It adapts the Orca self-development handoff (22 October 2026) to this repository, after checking each of its findings against CIVIC's code. The command described under [The command](#the-command) is built as `civic preview` ([decision 0021](decisions/0021-civic-preview-reviews-a-worktree-of-civic.md)); where this plan and that decision differ, the decision wins. The first trial is described under [What the trial showed](#what-the-trial-showed).

## Outcome

Open any CIVIC worktree's own canvas with one command, comment on it with CIVIC's overlay, hand the comment to an agent as a work request, have the agent fix it in its own worktree and show the fix on that worktree's own copy, and resolve it. The comments, the requests and the fixes are CIVIC's own records, filed on CIVIC's own lines and revisions ([decision 0020](decisions/0020-records-live-in-the-civic-folder.md)).

CIVIC makes no model calls and launches no agents ([decision 0006](decisions/0006-deterministic-civic-for-agentic-teams.md)). The coordinator in the Orca handoff is therefore not part of CIVIC. The agent is external (Orca, Claude Code or Codex, through the MCP server). CIVIC is where the work is seen, requested, re-captured and signed off.

## What exists today

- **One dev host, strict port.** `packages/local/start.mjs` starts a detached Vite server with hot module replacement (HMR) on `CIVIC_LOCAL_PORT` (3012 by default). It only checks that the port is free. It writes `runtime.json` with a pid, port, origin and start time: no source, store or mode. `packages/canvas/bin/civic-canvas.mjs` is a second launcher (3020, store `~/.civic/canvas`) and `packages/local/desktop-launch.mjs` a third, which I did not read.
- **State follows the checkout.** `packages/local/store.mjs` puts the store at `CIVIC_LOCAL_STORE`, else `CIVIC_STORE`, else `<launching checkout>/.civic-canvas/`. A worktree therefore starts with its own empty store.
- **A running instance exists.** `~/Projects/CIVIC/.civic-canvas/runtime.json` records pid 8839 on port 3012 with a tailnet origin, started 21 October. I did not check that it is alive and did not touch it. From its store's location it appears to serve the main checkout, so a change in another worktree would not show there until it is merged.
- **Nothing is packaged.** The Electron launcher is "not a signed, packaged application" (`packages/local/README.md`). There is no release build and no promotion step to keep apart.
- **The review loop already works on any loopback app.** `civic review-app` ([decision 0019](decisions/0019-review-a-running-app-through-a-proxy.md)) adds the overlay and registers the preview on the checkout's line. `civic claim`, `report-fix`, `recapture` and `resolve` finish the loop.
- **Setup is separate installs** in `graph/`, `review/`, `importers/`, `crawl/` and `packages/`. A fresh worktree has none. `packages/local/worktree-dependencies.mjs` refuses to install into a worktree for the user ("Install the worktree's pinned dependencies separately").

## What the trial showed

On 23 October, on ports 53965–53967 with a temporary store and a throwaway git repository, I started the standalone canvas on the Notebook example behind `civic review-app` and drove it with Chrome. The overlay loaded in the canvas page (the canvas draws its screens in that one page; no frames). An annotation on the "Notebook home" card was saved and `civic annotations` listed it on the repository's line. All processes were stopped afterwards by their recorded pids.

Not tried: the CIVIC repository's own `.civic/`, recapture or `report-fix` through the proxy, HMR through the proxy's WebSocket tunnel, Electron, and the running 3012 instance.

## The Orca findings, checked against CIVIC

| Orca finding | In CIVIC |
| --- | --- |
| F1 The dogfood route is an installation lifecycle | Differs. No release build exists. The likely gap is that the live instance serves the main checkout, so other worktrees' changes are invisible to it. |
| F2 Several launchers, no one open/attach contract | Applies, smaller: the host and canvas launchers I read share no identity, attach or readiness check. |
| F3 State follows the launching checkout | Applies: `.civic-canvas/` is per checkout. |
| F4 A responding port is not an identity | Applies: the port probe and `runtime.json` say nothing about source, store or mode. |
| F5 Restart policy, queues, effects | Mostly n/a: no engine holds queued work. What a restart can lose here is unsaved drafts, captures and comments (AGENTS.md says to keep them across navigation and resizing) and isolated live-run workers. |
| F6 Owner authentication | n/a. The host is loopback only with no sign-in. Recapture signs in with the preview's key file (`--bearer-file`), never copied into records. |
| F7 Worker isolation | n/a for CIVIC. It launches no workers. Each external agent uses its own worktree, and claims are per line. |
| F8 Preview, check and checkpoint tools | CIVIC is that host: `review-app`, `recapture`, `bin/signoff`. Reuse them. |
| F9 History is not a current pass | Applies. `plans/005` has a manual Electron check. No recorded acceptance of this loop exists. |

## The command

Match the Orca `pnpm preview` contract once that is in Orca's main (names below are placeholders): run from any CIVIC worktree, free ports, temporary data, one link, with `list`, `stop` and `link`.

- **start** (the default; repeating it attaches). Uses this worktree's source. Starts the canvas host on a free port, then `civic review-app` in front of it, registered on this worktree's line, filed under its branch. Prints one link, the proxy's `/review`. Default project: the Notebook example. `--project` picks another.
- **list** shows the instances and their worktrees, heads, ports and whether each is alive.
- **stop** ends one instance, or all, by the processes it recorded.
- **link** prints the link again.

How it behaves:

1. **Identity.** One instance per worktree, found in a registry under `$TMPDIR` (not in any checkout), with pid and start time of each process, ports, store, project, head and the dirty state at start.
2. **Attach only on a match.** Attach when the recorded processes are alive with the recorded start times and `/review` answers. Otherwise report a stale record and start fresh. A port held by anything else is refused, never killed or adopted.
3. **Two starts at once** end with one owner of each process (a lock in the registry).
4. **Stop** signals only recorded processes whose start times still match. No `pkill`, no stale pid trust. It never touches 3012 or `.civic-canvas/`.
5. **Data.** A temporary store per instance by default. Records of the review itself go to CIVIC's `.civic/` ([decision 0020](decisions/0020-records-live-in-the-civic-folder.md)).
6. **Setup.** If `node_modules` is missing, run `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` in the directories the command needs, in this worktree only (it is CIVIC's own checkout, not a connected app). This is an open decision below.
7. **Status shows what runs.** Head, whether the tree is dirty, and when the instance started. HMR serves uncommitted bytes, so head alone is not the running source.

## What each change needs to take effect

| Change | Takes effect by |
| --- | --- |
| Canvas and shell UI (`packages/canvas/src`, `packages/shell`) | Vite HMR. Verify through the proxy. |
| `civic`, `graph/`, `importers/`, `crawl/`, `review/` commands | The next command. |
| `review-app`, overlay and MCP servers | Restart that process. Records are untouched. |
| Vite plugin and host code (`canvas-host`, `vite-connector`, the review server) | Restart the host. Unsaved drafts, captures and comments must survive; to be verified. |
| Electron main and preload | Relaunch the window. |
| Dependencies | Install, then restart the host. |

## Safety

Everything in AGENTS.md holds. In particular: ephemeral ports, never the reserved ones; never change HOME; no recursive deletion outside owned, verified artifacts; no model calls; loopback only; keys out of logs; the running 3012 instance and its `.civic-canvas/` are not touched without the owner's approval.

## Slices

1. **Baseline, read-only.** Record the live instance's real state (is pid 8839 alive, what it serves) before anything changes.
2. **Start, attach, list, stop, link** with tests on temporary ports and a foreign listener.
3. **Activation.** Verify HMR and the WebSocket tunnel through the proxy; add the running-source status.
4. **Setup** from a fresh worktree.
5. **One real journey** (below).

## Acceptance

Each row is proved with current evidence, not by a past run.

| ID | Scenario | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S01 | Start from a fresh worktree | Link opens; overlay present; processes and ports recorded |
| S02 | Start again | Same instance; no new processes |
| S03 | Two starts at once | One owner per process |
| S04 | A foreign process holds the requested port | Refused; the process is still running and was sent nothing |
| S05 | Start from a second worktree | Its own instance and store; the first is untouched |
| S06 | Edit a canvas component | Visible change through the proxy without reload; HMR not broken by the tunnel |
| S07 | Edit host code | Host restart; the status says so; drafts survive |
| S08 | `stop` | Only recorded processes end; others stay |
| S09 | The 3012 instance | Same pid, port and `runtime.json` before and after |
| S10 | Comment on CIVIC's own UI | Annotation on this worktree's line and revision, in CIVIC's `.civic/` |
| S11 | The whole loop | Comment, request, an external agent claims it in its own worktree, `report-fix` with its own copy, recapture, the owner resolves |
| S12 | Merge, then the live instance | The change shows in 3012 only if the owner has asked for that; no restart without approval |

Record every step the owner or the agent had to do in a terminal. The target is none for routine runs.

## Follow-ups after `civic preview`

`civic preview` is built ([decision 0021](decisions/0021-civic-preview-reviews-a-worktree-of-civic.md)). Slices 2, 4 and part of 3 are done: start, attach, list, link and stop; setup from a fresh worktree; and hot reload through the proxy (S06). Still open:

1. **`--desktop`.** CIVIC's Electron shell needs the branch in its window title and its own profile (`packages/local/desktop.mjs`), and an Electron binary to verify them.
2. **The full agent loop (S11).** An external agent claims a request in its own worktree, reports a fix with a preview of its own copy, `civic recapture` checks it there, and the owner resolves it. The launcher passes the preview's access key file when it finds exactly one, but no recapture has been run through a preview.
3. **S12.** Merging to main and seeing the change in the owner's live instance on port 3012, only when the owner asks for it.
4. **Sign-in.** The preview has none (decision 0021, point 7).
5. **Fixture signing (done).** `bin/with-temp-root.mjs` tells git inside every check not to sign commits or tags, so no test file needs its own `commit.gpgsign` setting and checks no longer ask the owner's signing key.
6. **The remaining rows of the table** that no test or trial has covered: S07 (host edit with unsaved drafts), S09 beyond the one `ps` comparison, and the rest of S10 across several worktrees.

## Still to build: source-to-element and backend coverage

Owner, 15 November 2026. Both come after the follow-ups above, when CIVIC is the focus again.

1. **Source-to-element.** From an element selected on the canvas or through the review overlay, CIVIC finds the source file and line that rendered it. The reverse also works: from a source file or diff hunk, CIVIC highlights the elements it renders. Comments and work requests carry that location, so the agent starts in the right file. Try it on CIVIC's own screens first, then on Orca and the Laundry app. CIVIC stays model-free ([decision 0006](decisions/0006-deterministic-civic-for-agentic-teams.md)): it records the location, and the external agent makes the change.
2. **Backend coverage.** Coverage today means screens and journeys. Add the server side: which routes, handlers and RPCs each journey exercises, and which ones no journey reaches, so a covered screen cannot hide an untested backend path. Derive it from recorded runs ([decision 0009](decisions/0009-recorded-runs-as-evidence.md)) and the graph, not from hand-written lists.

Reference: [Gui](https://usegui.com) (open source, Apache 2.0, alpha) lets you select an element in a running React (Vite, Next.js) or Astro app and hands the change to your own agent, including ACP agents. Read how it maps elements to source; do not depend on it. Orca treats Gui as an outside integration, the way it treats CIVIC.

## Open decisions

1. The command's name. Follow Orca's final contract.
2. May the command install dependencies into CIVIC's own worktrees?
3. The default project: Notebook example, or a manifest for CIVIC itself.
4. Whether `civic` should eventually own the 3012 instance. Separate approval; nothing here touches it.
5. CIVIC already reviews itself as a workspace ("Isolated CIVIC", through `civic preview`). Making CIVIC a project in its own picker, with a scenario registry for its screens, is now needed so that source-to-element works on CIVIC's own UI.

## The brief to hand an executing session

# Effect App Server and Run Lifecycle - Plan

## Goal Capsule

- **Objective:** People can use the same local CIVIC workspace from Electron and a browser, close either safely, and recover their isolated runs after reopening.
- **Means:** An Effect application host around the existing canvas and run service, with XState lifecycle decisions (KTD1–KTD4).
- **Authority:** The user's agreed lifecycle below and CIVIC's accepted architecture decisions govern implementation. This document authorizes no deployment, remote exposure, project re-onboarding or external publication.
- **Ownership:** One implementing controller owns this worktree and integration. The primary checkout's startup, onboarding and Tailscale work remain owned by the other CIVIC chat.
- **Execution profile:** Characterize journal behavior before refactoring, then deliver the six dependency-ordered units. Use bounded local verification; keep provider calls at zero.
- **Stop conditions:** Stop for a changed core schema, weakened journal/evidence rule, incompatible dependency pin, conflicting checkout ownership, or a need to mutate the primary checkout or its installed stores.
- **Tail ownership:** The implementing controller owns packaging, local acceptance and documentation. Remote access and multiplayer remain later work.

---

## Product Contract

### Summary

Add a managed local app-server that Electron and browser clients share. Keep it running while at least one client remains attached, including a windowless Electron app until Quit. When the final client leaves, allow a short reconnection interval, drain accepted work within a deadline, preserve journals and release all workers and listeners.

### Problem Frame

The current canvas server's lifetime belongs to its launcher. The Vite connector creates the run service and calls its close method when its HTTP server closes. Individual runs already have isolation, serialized operations and recovery journals, but there is no application-client ownership layer to decide when the shared process should exit.

A launcher-owned child can disappear while another client still needs it. A process with no client ownership can remain indefinitely after all apps close. The new host must distinguish those cases without changing what a completed run operation proves.

### Key Decisions

- **Same Mac first.** Independent Electron and browser clients share one local workspace; other devices and multiplayer follow later. Governs R1, R11. (session-settled: user-directed — chosen over remote-device or team access now: validate the local lifecycle first.)
- **Electron counts until Quit.** Governs R2. (session-settled: user-directed — chosen over last-window closure: an app still running in the Dock retains its connection.)
- **Preserve the existing core.** Governs R7–R10. (session-settled: user-approved — chosen over a replacement SQLite record store: the graph, journal and Git synchronization contracts already exist.)

### Requirements

**Application lifetime**

- R1. Compatible Electron and browser clients using the same canonical canvas store attach to one local app-server.
- R2. Electron main retains its client connection until actual Quit; closing or crashing a renderer alone does not release it.
- R3. Each top-level CIVIC browser tab retains its own client connection, including while hidden; preview frames, capture browsers and run workers do not retain the server independently.
- R4. Reloads and brief disconnects receive a bounded reconnection interval; expired clients cannot retain a server indefinitely.
- R5. After the final client expires, the host refuses new work, drains previously accepted work within a bounded deadline, closes resources and exits.
- R6. Quitting the launcher that created the server never stops it while another client remains; a reconnect after shutdown begins waits for a fresh server.

**Run and core integrity**

- R7. Preserve the graph, review records, signed `RecordsRemote` synchronization and the distinct Proposal, Decision, Adoption and Verification records.
- R8. Preserve version-1 run journals, completed-operation reconstruction, same-source checks, synthetic credentials, per-run isolation and intent-based duplicate-write receipts.
- R9. Incomplete or failed operations never become successful observations, completed journal entries or passing replay evidence.
- R10. Preserve the existing run takeover lease, expected synthetic actor checks, input validation, worker limits and idle-expiry behavior.

**Compatibility and scope**

- R11. Bind managed servers to loopback and retain existing origin, authentication and project-binding checks; a presence connection conveys no new record permissions.
- R12. Pin Effect `4.0.5`, `@effect/platform-node` `4.0.5` and XState `6.0.0-alpha.69`, matching Orca at research time.
- R13. Keep the current app adapters, canvas, programmatic host exports, recorder format and installed-from-Git integration working.
- R14. Opening a stopped workspace requires Electron or the local launcher; browser-only automatic wakeup and unattended background work are outside this delivery.

### Acceptance Examples

| ID | Situation | Required outcome |
|---|---|---|
| AE1 | Electron and browser share a workspace; Electron quits | Browser and its run continue. Covers R1, R6. |
| AE2 | Last Electron window closes, then the app later quits | Window closure retains the server; Quit releases Electron's hold. Covers R2. |
| AE3 | Last browser tab reloads within the grace period | Same server instance survives; the tab reattaches. Covers R3, R4. |
| AE4 | Final client closes during a mutation | New work is refused after draining begins; a result is either recorded fully or left incomplete, never invented. Covers R5, R8, R9. |
| AE5 | A completed mutation's response is lost, then the run reopens | Same intent returns its recorded receipt without another write in the reconstructed run. Covers R8. |
| AE6 | A second page reopens a run, then the old page closes | The stale close does not stop the new owner's run. Covers R10. |
| AE7 | Reopen after a source change or a journal result mismatch | Recovery is refused visibly; old evidence remains available. Covers R8, R9. |
| AE8 | All clients crash, or the launcher dies before attaching | Client expiry or startup timeout closes the host; no permanent orphan. Covers R4, R5. |

### Scope Boundaries

This delivery covers managed server discovery, client presence, run lifecycle supervision, a minimal Electron shell, browser integration and local acceptance. It retains the current project picker's single selected compilation binding. A project switch remains an explicit viewer restart, not an implicit change to another tab's active run.

Deferred: simultaneous independently compiled projects within one host, remote-device access, live team synchronization, presence UI, shared driving, offline collaborative editing, packaged installers and auto-update. Existing permitted proxy behavior remains supported by the low-level host, but this work does not configure or widen it.

The core stays deterministic and provider-free under decision 0006. Existing CLI and MCP record actions keep their permissions and do not become implicit background-server owners.

---

## Planning Contract

### Current Architecture and Research

Grounded at `baseline_commit`. Re-anchor before implementation if the branch changes.

| Existing source | Constraint carried forward |
|---|---|
| `packages/canvas/server/runtime-service.mjs` | One worker per run; eight-worker cap; per-run queue; 30-second worker-call timeout; 30-minute idle expiry; journal before/after changing operations. |
| `packages/canvas/server/runtime-service.check.mjs` | Existing recovery, fresh credentials, stale-close protection and duplicate-intent scenarios are compatibility checks. |
| `packages/vite-connector/src/review-plugin.mjs` | Owns project binding and source refresh; HTTP close currently triggers unawaited run cleanup. |
| `packages/shell/server/review-server.mjs` | Owns session/bearer authentication, exact-origin checks, project routing and recording/replay persistence. |
| `packages/canvas/src/runtime-session.ts` | Browser restores synthetic state and sends lease-bound run close. |
| `packages/canvas/server/canvas-host.mjs` | Existing `runtime` injection seam and programmatic host API can support managed ownership. |
| `review/src/store.ts`, `review/src/remote.ts`, `review/src/sync.ts` | Record storage and signed Git synchronization already exist; they are not replaced. |
| `docs/decisions/0004-graph-first-journey-engine-as-viewer.md`, `docs/decisions/0008-team-records-on-a-git-ref.md`, `docs/decisions/0009-recorded-runs-as-evidence.md` | Graph ownership, remote semantics and tape-versus-evidence boundaries remain authoritative. |

OpenCode was inspected at commit `214fb7fdbab9ad13773629839f1178382400cf97` on 2026-10-18. Its current source has moved beyond older desktop sidecar paths. Borrow the following mechanisms, not its daemon lifetime or its application domain:

- [Service discovery and ensure](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/214fb7fdbab9ad13773629839f1178382400cf97/packages/client/src/effect/service.ts): private registration, authenticated health checks and compatibility-aware reuse shape KTD3.
- [Desktop background connection](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/214fb7fdbab9ad13773629839f1178382400cf97/packages/desktop/src/main/service/background-service-state.ts): startup consumers await a shared connection outcome; renderer startup need not own service creation. Shapes U5.
- [Server process](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/214fb7fdbab9ad13773629839f1178382400cf97/packages/server/src/process.ts): explicit starting/stopping status and scoped application cleanup shape KTD2 and KTD5.
- [Bounded event feed](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/214fb7fdbab9ad13773629839f1178382400cf97/packages/server/src/event-feed.ts): subscriber cleanup and explicit overflow shape KTD6.

[OpenCode's server documentation](https://docs.opencode.ai/docs/server/) confirms the shared API plus event-stream client model. It does not establish CIVIC's last-client shutdown policy. [XState's execution model](https://stately.ai/docs/xstate/v6/how-xstate-runs-machines) supports pure transitions separated from effect execution. Use APIs verified against the pinned packages, not older Effect 3 examples or newer alpha features.

### Key Technical Decisions

- KTD1. **Keep the host inside `@civic/canvas`.** Add server-only modules and an `./app-server` export rather than another core or contracts package. Retain `startCanvas` as an embeddable low-level host; the managed launcher wraps it. Effect and XState stay out of `graph/`, `review/` and the browser bundle. Implements R7, R12, R13.
- KTD2. **One serialized lifecycle owner.** XState computes server and run state transitions; Effect owns real timers, queues, listeners and workers. Lifecycle snapshots are transient. Durable run facts continue to live in the existing journal, with no second workflow database. Implements R5, R8–R10.
- KTD3. **Discover, authenticate, then adopt.** Canonicalize the store path and keep an instance registration with PID, instance nonce, build/protocol identity and loopback endpoint in a private file. Elect the owner with an atomic per-store lock directory containing an exclusive owner record; retain it for the host's lifetime. Serialize recovery through a separate breaker claim and recheck ownership before admitting a winner. Recovery requires positive evidence that the recorded same-machine owner is dead; age, missed heartbeats or a failed health request alone never license takeover. Missing or unreadable ownership fails closed with a repair instruction. Refuse a live incompatible owner or unrelated listener instead of killing it or opening a second writer. Registration removal and lock release must match the exiting instance nonce. Implements R1, R6, R11, R13.
- KTD4. **Use renewable connections, not a decrement-only counter.** Track server-issued client IDs with connection generations. Desktop main authenticates with a private local capability; browser tickets are issued through the existing authenticated review middleware and permit only browser presence. Browser tickets are single-use, expire after 10 seconds and travel as a WebSocket subprotocol value, never in URLs or logs. Upgrades validate the exact route, trusted origin and ticket or desktop capability before retaining the host. Desktop connections without a browser Origin require the local capability and loopback transport. Validate message schemas and cap incoming frames at 16 KiB. Late releases from an old generation do nothing. Implements R2–R4, R11.
- KTD5. **Bound every unattended interval.** Initial defaults: first-client deadline 60 seconds; transport ping every 5 seconds; missing-client expiry 15 seconds; final-client grace 10 seconds; shutdown drain 30 seconds followed by up to 5 seconds for resource closure. These are internal, injectable test constants, not new user settings. Existing worker-call and run-idle limits remain per R10. A final client may therefore leave up to 45 seconds of grace and shutdown work, or up to 60 seconds after abrupt loss is detected through expiry, while the machine and event loop are running. Sleep does not create a hard real-time guarantee. Implements R4, R5.
- KTD6. **Keep operation HTTP routes; add one control socket.** The socket carries lifecycle status and run invalidations, with a bounded queue of 256 messages of at most 16 KiB per client. Full state is fetched through existing authenticated reads after reconnect; overflow closes the socket and requires resynchronization. No journal, raw form values, credentials or captures are broadcast. The server only emits a completed-operation notification after its journal receipt is saved. Implements R8, R9, R11, R13.
- KTD7. **Make shutdown one-way.** Reattachment cancels `Waiting`, but cannot cancel `Stopping`. A root shutdown first fences new operations and run creation, including in-flight startup/restore continuations. Accepted run queues drain under KTD5; finalizers then explicitly terminate workers and await closure. Journals are retained. One native root deadline watchdog outside the cancellable run scope exits the host with a failure outcome if cooperative cleanup exceeds the final deadline; no extra supervisor process is introduced. The deadline assumes a responsive event loop, per KTD5. Implements R5, R6, R8, R9.
- KTD8. **Keep the app connection independent of Vite generations.** Effect owns one stable Node HTTP listener, the control socket and server identity. The managed viewer runs Vite in middleware mode behind that listener, with HMR attached to the parent listener; its restart replaces only the viewer generation. Starting and stopping responses are explicit while ordinary review routes are unavailable. Add an awaitable generation-disposal hook rather than relying on Vite's `httpServer` close event, which is absent in middleware mode. Project/source changes retain existing refusal semantics; they never rebind an old run to new code. Implements R6, R10, R13.

Keep registration and its capability under the canonical store's `.review-data/service/`, with directory mode `0700` and file mode `0600`; do not write it into a reviewed app or a Git record. This is ephemeral local connection state, not a second product store.

Add exact dependencies to the owning canvas package and lockfile: the R12 pins plus `ws` `8.22.0` and development types `@types/ws` `8.18.2`, matching Orca. The Electron development dependency is `44.9.0`, also matching Orca. `@xstate/effect` `1.0.0-alpha.8` is recorded for comparison but is unnecessary for the chosen pure-transition host, so do not add an unused bridge. Use Effect 4 `Context.Service`, layers and scoped resource acquisition where services earn a boundary.

### High-Level Technical Design

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Desktop[Electron main: lifetime owner] --> Host[Effect app-server scope]
    Browser[Top-level browser tab] --> Host
    Host --> Viewer[Existing Vite canvas and review middleware]
    Host --> Runs[Run service supervisor]
    Runs --> Workers[Isolated run workers]
    Runs --> Journals[Existing version-1 journals]
    Viewer --> Core[Existing graph and review APIs]
    Core --> Git[Existing records and Git remote]
```

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Starting
    Starting --> Serving: ready and client attached
    Starting --> AwaitingClient: ready without client
    Starting --> Stopping: startup failure or boot deadline
    AwaitingClient --> Serving: first client attaches
    AwaitingClient --> Stopping: first-client deadline
    Serving --> Waiting: final client lost
    Waiting --> Serving: client attaches before deadline
    Waiting --> Stopping: grace expires
    Serving --> Stopping: explicit host termination signal
    Stopping --> Stopped: bounded drain and cleanup
    Stopped --> [*]
```

`AwaitingClient` uses the first-client deadline in KTD5; `Waiting` uses the final-client grace. Bound the initial host boot itself to 60 seconds, and start the first-client deadline when readiness is published. Client counts and grace timers are rebuilt after process restart, never loaded from persisted XState snapshots.

The run machine has `Starting`, `Restoring`, `Ready`, `Executing`, `Stopping` and `Stopped` states. Its transient stop reason distinguishes explicit closure, expiry, worker failure and host shutdown; it is not a new graph record. Source mismatch refuses commands without pretending that the old run has become current. A stop fence prevents any pending start or restore from publishing a usable run after shutdown begins.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Host
    participant Run
    participant Journal
    participant Worker
    Client->>Host: changing operation with existing intent identity
    Host->>Run: admit before stop fence
    Run->>Journal: save incomplete entry
    Run->>Worker: execute
    Client--xHost: final client disconnects
    Host->>Host: grace expires; fence new work
    Worker-->>Run: result before drain deadline
    Run->>Journal: save completed result
    Run-->>Host: settle accepted operation
    Host->>Worker: terminate and await exit
    Host->>Host: close host resources; remove own registration
```

If the worker or persistence misses the deadline, no completed receipt is acknowledged. Existing failure cleanup may remove the failed entry; any surviving incomplete entry follows R9 and the existing recovery rule below. No completion event is fabricated. Emit success only after the operation's final source check as well as persistence; a source change after persistence yields a stale-state notification, not successful runtime evidence.

### Journal Compatibility Rules

R8 and R9 preserve the following behavior of `runtime-service.mjs`:

1. Reopening reconstructs a fresh isolated backend from its seed and complete journal entries. It deliberately re-executes those synthetic operations and compares their results; it is not continuation of an arbitrary process or an exactly-once external-effect engine.
2. Incomplete entries are excluded during restore, as today. The page's unconfirmed step remains available for explicit resend. Do not automatically retry an uncertain operation against a surviving worker.
3. A completed mutation with an intent returns its recorded result for the same operation and synthetic actor. Different arguments or actors using that identity are refused; reset forgets data and intent receipts together.
4. Preserve the journal path, version, seed, clock, timezone and source binding. Credential regeneration and sensitive-payload checks remain in place.
5. Completion is acknowledged only after persistence succeeds. A failed persistence cannot be converted into a successful client result or replay pass.

Atomic rename gives the existing process-recovery behavior; this plan does not add a power-loss durability or filesystem-fsync guarantee. Unexported browser recording steps cannot be recovered from a server journal that never received them.

See [the review store](../review#lines).

Acceptance: an annotation made in one worktree is claimed by an agent in another, the reported fix is re-captured on that worktree's preview with no model call, and the request resolves through its lane.

## 3. Typed contract and change records

Start with the Decision record alone, because the gate (step 8) needs a stored, owned decision to stop flagging a conflict a person already decided. Then store Proposal, Adoption, and Verification as separate, owned records, along with the collaboration record types (Ambiguity, Constraint, Coverage gap, Divergence, Risk, Exception). Alignment states read from records instead of being recomputed.

The journey engine already has working examples: `coverage.json` is a Coverage gap record with versioned write-back, and its coverage candidates are proposals that never count as adoption.

The Decision record is built in [`graph/`](../graph#decisions). A conflict keeps what the import raised, and its status, classification and alignment state are read from the Decision in force on it. A changed call supersedes the earlier decision instead of overwriting it, and an agent can't write one (D35). Each demo keeps its decisions in a `civic.decisions/0` file next to its contract, and `civic decide` records a new one after checking it against the graph. The gate counts a conflict as decided only when a Decision is in force on it, so the Button's brand outline conflict fails on the raised graph and passes once its decision is recorded.

Progress, 2026-10-12: the decision loop is built ([`graph/`](../graph#the-decision-loop)). Proposal, Adoption and Verification are separate records in the same decision file, written by `civic propose`, `civic adopt` and `civic verify` after a check against the graph. A decision names the proposal it approves, and an `update-contract` decision must approve one. Each decided fix has a stage read from its records: awaiting adoption, adopted, verified (the conflict then reads aligned), failed or regressed. The gate re-checks every fix on every run. It blocks when an import that read the adopted revision still raises the conflict, when a verification fails, and when evidence a verification cited fails later; unadopted and unverified fixes and undecided proposals are advisory. A re-import that no longer raises an adopted conflict settles it, and its records stay in the file as history. Agents may propose and record an adoption but never verify (D35). The collaboration record types (Ambiguity, Constraint, Coverage gap, Divergence, Risk, Exception) are still to come.

Progress, 2026-10-12: alignment states are read from records. `civic alignment` gives each semantic component one state on each platform that implements it, from its conflicts and the decisions in force, the fix stages, exceptions and accepted limitations, and its evidence. A platform without a passing run is unknown, never aligned. See [`graph/`](../graph#alignment-civic-alignment).

Generalize the `@civic/shell` adapter boundary now that Fluent is a second consumer ([decision 0003](decisions/0003-civic-shell-package.md) was paused until then). Follow the v4 handoff's onboarding direction: a local project manifest plus a supported web adapter.

Discover the app by crawling first (D34): one CIVIC crawl loop, on Playwright for web and Appium for native, explores from seeded fixtures with destructive actions blocked, and groups states by DOM or accessibility hierarchy. Crawled states come in as discovered until a person confirms them. Write or generate an adapter only where a crawl can't tell states apart, reach them, or reset them. Add the frame walk (D33): the scenario player walks imported design frames along their prototype links, labelled as design intent.

Validate onboarding with two cases ([onboarding and ingestion](onboarding-and-ingestion.md#6-validating-onboarding)): the Fluent Button, and Example's five unmapped destination states brought in through the manifest as expected states.

Acceptance: a second small web app connects without importing Example code, unsupported features stay visibly unavailable, and source refresh, capture, and replay make zero model calls with providers disabled.

It onboarded the engine's manifest-free example as a [second app](../projects/discovery-app): 4 screens and 6 paths, all discovered until a person confirms them in a confirmation file, which can also declare journeys for the shape checks. The gate reports unconfirmed screens as advisory. Still to come: an Appium driver for native and the frame walk (D33).

Progress, 2026-10-12: the canvas reads the graph. `civic screen` answers what the graphs know about one screen, and the journey canvas's Contract panel shows it for the selected screen: run evidence with the failing tests, paths on, and the gate's findings marked new or baselined. The engine runs CIVIC's CLI for it, as it does for shared annotations, so neither imports the other.

It is tested against a stand-in server on Android and iOS sources and against a real Appium 3 server with Appium's fake driver. No emulator or device runs in the cloud, so no native app has been crawled yet. Native crawls can't block network writes the way the web driver does, so they need a test build. CIVIC's crawl drivers (Playwright and Appium) are its interaction drivers; a runtime and data adapter for native apps is still to come.

## 5. Identity, permissions, and multiplayer

Real identities, scoped permissions, and versioned shared records, following the spec's [multiplayer boundary](product-spec.md#multiplayer-and-ownership). The single local access key and the portal's collaborator access are not this model.

Progress, 2026-10-12: shared records are versioned and permissions are scoped. Each work request counts its changes. A write that names the version it read (`<id>@<version>`, as `civic requests` and `civic queue` print it) is refused if the request changed since then, naming the change, and nothing is written. `civic.access.json` on the default branch gives each person the read, write, approve and resolve scopes. An agent has its person's scopes, and the graph's rules still stop it from resolving. Still to come: the team-wide store, which brings authenticated identities.

Progress, 2026-10-12 ([decision 0008](decisions/0008-team-records-on-a-git-ref.md)): `civic sync` shares each person's store with the team through `refs/civic/records` on the repository's remote, behind a remote interface that a hosted service can implement later. The merge goes record by record. Comments made at once are both kept, and any other change made on both sides is set aside as a conflict for a person to settle. Shared changes are checked against `civic.access.json` before they're merged. Progress, 2026-10-12: signed syncs. `civic keygen` gives each person an Ed25519 key, and `civic.access.json` lists their public keys. Once any key is listed, a shared sync counts only when a key listed for the person it names signs it. The trailer stops being a mere claim. ## 6. Journey completeness and replay

Add fixture capture to `bin/signoff` so evidence can be regenerated and becomes visibly stale. Then add replay from start to the scenario player, and native captures as runners allow.

Discovery and replay are deterministic by default. Record journeys with existing Playwright tooling (Codegen, the reporter API, traces) instead of building a recorder, and replay only verified paths, stopping visibly on a miss. Report counts and denominators rather than confidence percentages. CIVIC makes no model calls (D30).

Acceptance: ordinary refresh and replay make zero model calls with providers disabled, and failed or cancelled operations never become successful edges.

Progress, 2026-10-12: evidence becomes visibly stale. A freshness rule in `civic.check.json` says which evidence proves code in this repository and where that code is. The gate reports evidence whose code changed since its revision as advisory, with a count, and `civic screen` and the journey canvas's Contract panel mark it. `bin/signoff --capture` recaptures Example's evidence when it's stale and stops so the new evidence is reviewed and committed. Still to come: replay from start in the scenario player, and native captures.

Progress, 2026-10-12: replay from start is built for project adapters. In the Inspect panel, "Replay from start" opens a fresh run at the journey's first screen and walks the shortest chain of declared paths to the selected screen, clicking each path's action by its accessible name and waiting for the adapter to land where the path says. A missing control or a wrong landing stops the replay with an alert naming the step, and nothing past it is claimed. Only the app's own transitions are captured, so a failed save never becomes an edge. Example's towel journey keeps its own player. Still to come: native captures.

Progress, 2026-10-12: the v7 handoff adds a deterministic recorder with saved, downloadable runs that replay from the same seed and stop on drift ([v7 notes](../packages/canvas/README.md#v7-handoff-update)). ## 7. Repository hygiene

## 8. The gate: `civic check`

One command that runs every check on a graph (contract conflicts, override drift, completeness, gaps) and exits non-zero when there are new findings nobody has decided. A baseline file records existing findings so old debt doesn't block a change. It prints a short Markdown summary and can post a `civic` commit status the way `bin/signoff` does, with no GitHub Actions. This is the SonarQube shape from [decision 0005](decisions/0005-what-civic-is.md): a finding is raised at the change that caused it.

Acceptance: on the Fluent Button and Card demo graphs, `civic check` fails on an undecided conflict, passes once a recorded decision covers it, ignores baselined findings, and reports counts with denominators. It makes no model calls.

Built in [`graph/`](../graph#the-gate-civic-check) and run by `bin/signoff` on the graphs in [`civic.check.json`](../civic.check.json). Undecided findings block: open conflicts, overrides no conflict tracks, expired exceptions, failing evidence, missing product states, dead ends and unreachable screens. Recorded facts and evidence debt (variants mapped to `none`, platform-only variants, missing run evidence, unconfirmed links, approved exceptions) are reported without blocking, and a project can choose its own list. The Card's undecided selectable override, its missing empty and error states, and the Checkout journey's dead end and unreachable screen are in [`civic.baseline.json`](../civic.baseline.json). Decisions come from Decision records (step 3).

## 9. Real inputs replace the stand-ins

The Figma importers already read the real `GET /v1/files/:key` export shape; what's missing is real files. This cloud environment can't reach Figma, so the founder exports the [Microsoft Fluent Android](https://www.figma.com/community/file/836835062056249539/microsoft-fluent-android) Community file with a personal access token (steps in the [Button demo](../demo/fluent-button/README.md)). Progress, 2026-10-11: the Button demo reads the real Android kit export. The kit predates Figma variants and draws only Primary and Text buttons, so there is no Neutral button to conflict with. The real conflict runs the other way: Compose ships `OutlinedButton` (Brand outline) and the kit doesn't draw it.

Progress, 2026-10-12: the demos read real Fluent 2 kits, trimmed to what they use. The Card's library file is the Fluent 2 Web kit, and the Button's iOS side reads the Fluent 2 iOS kit, which raises two conflicts: iOS ships Danger and Transparent neutral buttons the kit doesn't draw. The Card raises three more where iOS `CardView` can't build library-default content (body, footer, header action). Fluent is the demo's example design system, not one CIVIC's team owns, so illustrative decisions settle all five: the iOS kit gains a Danger button, Transparent neutral stays iOS-only, iOS `CardView` gains a body slot, and iOS goes without the footer and header action as an accepted limitation. The Shop product file stays illustrative. Example's review suite is 39 of 39 passing after stale tests were fixed.

## 10. Checks where each role works

Part 2 of [decision 0005](decisions/0005-what-civic-is.md): raise each finding at the change that caused it, in the tool where that change lives ([onboarding and ingestion, 4d](onboarding-and-ingestion.md#4d-raising-violations-and-drift-to-the-right-roles)). Today the gate posts one `civic` commit status, and its summary is read only by whoever runs `bin/signoff`.

- **Find the side that moved.** Compare each side with the last revision where they agreed, ask the owner of the change that introduced the difference, and tell the other side's owners. *Built:* `civic check --since <ref>` compares with the merge base ([graph README](../graph/README.md#the-gate-civic-check)).
- **Engineering:** a pull request check whose summary lists the new findings with their owners, through the same local signoff and no GitHub Actions. *Built:* `bin/signoff` puts that summary on the open pull request as one comment, edited in place, beside the `civic` status.
- **QA:** a Playwright reporter that writes run evidence into the graph and prints the scenarios a run left uncovered. *Built:* `CivicReporter` in [`importers/`](../importers/README.md) writes a `civic.run/0` file and prints what now fails, what now passes and what was left uncovered, with QA owners; the Button demo's web suite runs it.
- **Design Engineering:** a check on a library release that names the variants left without a mapping and the product overrides the release breaks. *Built:* `civic release --since <ref>`, printed by `bin/signoff`.
- **Design:** findings on a Figma frame wait for the Figma plugin ([later](#later-not-scheduled)); until then they reach designers through the review loop. Example's designers work in Claude Design and Open Design, so its design input (see [order of work](#order-of-work)) comes first.

Acceptance: a change to one side of the Button or Card raises its finding on that change only, names who is asked and who is told, and makes no model calls.

# Delegation protocol

Delegate only when isolated context, specialization, useful parallelism, or disposable exploration outweighs coordination. Otherwise root works. Root remains controller, integrator, and completion owner. Each child satisfies one named evidence/signoff need rather than duplicating root work. A child has no controller, integration, landing, external-action, completion, or delegation authority.

Read-only is default. A mutation lease names its isolated worktree or paths, permitted edits and commands, required check, and stop condition. Independent isolated worktrees may hold concurrent bounded mutation leases only when their paths, decisions, dependencies, integration targets, landing surfaces, authority, and external effects do not overlap. A shared worktree has one writer. Root waits for every mutating lease to close before it integrates, lands, changes phase, operates on worktrees, or completes.

Before dispatch record goal, active stage, source or path, expected benefit, mode, ownership, allowed commands, forbidden paths or actions, named evidence/signoff need, required verification, and stop condition. An assessment is read-only evidence, not mutation authority. A child may not change instructions, provider state, configuration outside its lease, commit, push, merge, publish, use credentials, act externally, or delegate.

On crossed scope, competing ownership, or unauthorized action: interrupt, inspect status and diff, preserve unrelated work, and reject unverified output. Root verifies accepted evidence and the final diff.

Pass only needed context and use only completed results. A child stops when that need is met or its assignment ends. Return only conclusion or diff summary, evidence, verification, uncertainty, and blockers.
# Lifecycle protocol

## Durable goals

Root creates or reuses goals only for multi-step, long-running, or restart-prone work. Goals record progress, never authority. Keep simple tasks goal-free. Complete only when no required work remains; block only after safe in-scope alternatives are exhausted.

## Plans

Keep plans concise, ordered, and in scope. Record controller, stage, authoritative artifact, owners, approval boundary, stop condition, and open questions. Plans may select tools and bounded workers, never broaden authority. One writer owns each worktree.

Execute accepted plans. Ask only at explicit gates for material product, scope, authority, risk, irreversible, external-effect, or user-owned choices. Reconcile when evidence requires a material scope or risk change.

## Execution economics

Before durable goal or plan work, root checks fresh capability and metering evidence already in context.

Record available harness and model CLIs; metering class; remaining quota and reset; historical actual cost or tokens; privacy and organization constraints; required capability and reasoning; source class, observation time, and freshness.

Unavailable or stale evidence is unknown. Missing telemetry alone does not block. History is not a future estimate. Root owns model, effort, and provider choice. Management does not collect telemetry or invoke providers.

## Controller ownership

Root remains controller, sole integrator, and completion owner. One lifecycle or stage controller is active at a time. Bounded workers do not inherit control. Reject overlapping lifecycle, planning, writing, delegation, integration, or landing ownership.

## Handoffs

A controller handoff requires a verified checkpoint naming the outgoing controller, completed stage, authoritative artifact and accepted findings, incoming controller, scope changes, outgoing-controller inactivity, and verification owner. Root verifies that checkpoint before activation. Informational handoffs transfer no authority.

## Review findings

Review findings are candidate evidence, not automatic work. Discovery importance and blocker eligibility are independent. Only blocks-now findings backed by evidence already anchored in the verified current revision may interrupt; observed evidence cannot admit its own block. The boundary criterion includes authority, safety, destructive action, and external effect. Decision-required is terminal and claim-scoped, creates no pending proposal, and leaves unrelated work running. Deferred findings do not change the active contract. One focused rereview after admitted repairs is the maximum current-stage loop.

Model or reasoning effort never changes scope, authority, verification obligations, or blocker eligibility.

## Reconciliation

After approved artifact changes, reconcile downstream plans before mutation. At each stage boundary confirm outcome, state, verification, approval boundary, and next action. Goals, plans, and handoffs never authorize publishing, destructive work, credentials, or external action.
# VCS

Inspect status/diff,upstream/divergence,remote/base/head,dup-PR/auth; preserve unrelated; hunk-stage.
Branch {repo rule;team=`<conventional-type>/<forge-username>/<short-kebab-summary>`;solo=`<conventional-type>/<short-kebab-summary>`;trusted repo/forge, not email;no agent/model/harness/vendor prefix;published: authority}.
Commit {discover repo format/limit first;lines <= limit, 100 if absent;subject-only/wrap;hooks enforce/not discover;commit auth != push}.

Concern commits; generated+source. Prepush: fold same-concern correction into owner commit; no trailing fixup. Postpush: additive iff independent|required|no scoped rewrite authority.

Map{lightweight;stale=scope change|CI repair/test/simplify/complete prior|later same-concern|gen/dependency move|post-PR}. Gates{prepush|stable/pre-final-CI|final handoff/readiness}: inspect{range,status/diff,upstream/divergence,later/earlier}; classify{independent,fixup,squash,obsolete}. Provisional CI push != ready; F/S/O blocks only when commit history is review input.
Unpushed rewrite iff {current task;unpublished/unshared;one owner;no prior-user/unrelated;same scope/tree/evidence;unprotected;repo allows}; finish grants no commit/landing. Else ask.
Pushed repair: direct user task/correction request authorizes owner fixup; no second ask. Require {current unprotected single-owner task branch;lease match;no tag/shared/prior-user/unrelated rewrite;requested scope/tree;rerun invalidated checks}; else ask exact branch/map. Reconcile once; force-with-lease; verify remote head. No proposed count-only/squash-merge rewrite.

Confirmed PR URL/base/head/draft first after repo gates; CI/review/long/monitor separate/bounded.
Push=>one current-head batch. Wait terminal unless unsafe/costly/harmful/stuck/user-now: {success/failure/cancel/timeout/dependency-skip}; no indefinite fail-fast wait. Classify product/infra/flaky; dedupe; one local repair pre-edit; invalidated+mandatory checks; history once; verify tree/history; push once. New head=>new batch.
